Data Science Tools (WS 2025/26)

Chapter 5 RGui

The R installed under Windows (similar under MacOS and Linux) contains a simple Graphical User Interface (GUI) for elementary data analysis and programming; the following

The GUI known as RGui consists of the following components:

Permanent

  1. Header bar (with common and partly panel-specific elements such as File, Edit, View, Help, Miscellaneous, Packages, Windows, Help) and context-sensitive buttons (e.g. STOP in console mode).
  2. Console (bottom left) for program input and output.

Optional

  1. Simple editor (create new script with file \(\rightarrow\)), R commands are transferred to the console with Ctrl-R and executed.
  2. Graphics windows (are opened implicitly with graphics commands, explicitly with R command windows()).

The R interpreter can be installed in English or German; in the English version, of course, the labels change, e.g. File instead of Datei.

5.1 Important R commands for help (within R)

R is a very complex piece of software in which you can only find your way around if you use the various help functions.

In the following list, only some of the function calls that can be entered in the console are shown as examples. The corresponding result is always suppressed and in some cases (e.g. with help.search("lm")) cannot be embedded in R Markdown at all, as a dedicated panel (for help.search("lm"), for example, the Help panel in RStudio) is used for output.

The console is available in R command line mode, in RGui as well as in the RStudio development environment described below.

The library function is used to display all installed R packages and localize all library paths:

> library()

If you use the function library with a package name as the first argument, the corresponding library is loaded and placed in the search path directly after the global environment. For example, the following function call loads the R package mlr (a very extensive collection of machine learning algorithms, and even more in the successor package mlr3, ).

> library(mlr)

Calling help with a function name as argument returns a function-specific help, here for lm:

> help("lm")

The function help.search is used to search the very extensive R help for a term. The following function call to search for print functions returns a very comprehensive result:

> help.search("print")

The arguments of a function14 are displayed with args, here for matrix:

> args("matrix")

And the body of a function is displayed with body, here for matrix:

> body("matrix")

With example the examples given in the documentation for a function are executed; here for mean:

> example("mean")

The quotation marks can often be omitted, e.g. example(mean) returns the same result as example("mean") .

With vignette all vignettes of the packages installed on the running system (with detailed explanations) are displayed:

> vignette()

If you also enter the vignette name (sometimes, but not always the library name15) in vignette, you will receive the corresponding vignette directly. Here is an example for the Tidyverse library dplyr:

> vignette("dplyr")

If no vignette exists for a library, a warning message indicating the lack of availability is displayed in the console, e.g. with vignette("tidyverse").

With apropos, all available and visible objects within the search path that use the object name specified in the argument or contain it as a character string are listed. Here as an example lm:

> apropos("lm")

The methods function is used both to identify class-specific functions (methods) of a specific class and to identify the class-specific functions associated with a generic function.

When specifying the class argument, the methods function outputs the names of all class-specific methods that are available for the object class named in the argument. Here is an example for lm:

> methods(class="lm")

If you call methods with a generic function name as default (generic.function), all methods belonging to the function argument are listed. The following call lists all methods that can be called generically via the print function:

> methods("print")

The function where from the R library pryr can be used to find both the environment and the installation directory of the library in which the symbol name specified for the default argument name can be found. Example: The following function call outputs both the library and the installation location of the function tally. Note that only the loaded packages are taken into account in the search16:

> pryr::where("tally")

The function find from the R package utils finds the package in the search path in which the symbol named as argument is available.

> find("tally")

The function sessionInfo from the R base package utils returns the encoding used locally in the current session, all libraries used, etc:

> sessionInfo()

The session_info function from the devtools package is a variant of utils::sessionInfo and outputs the same information in a somewhat clearer form – however, within RStudio (not within Rgui) an uncritical collision currently occurs with a parallel installation of Quarto:

> devtools::session_info()

If a library name (of an installed library) is used as an argument in the session_info function, all associated dependencies are output. Here is an example for ggplot2:

> devtools::session_info("ggplot2")

library loads a package that is placed immediately after the global environment (.GlobalEnv) in the search path (diagnosable with search()) when the library name alone is mentioned without any additional arguments. The following example loads the string processing package stringr:

> library(stringr)

ls() alone lists all symbols stored in the workspace .GlobalEnv; this corresponds to ls(".GlobalEnv").

> ls()

If you want to list all exported symbols of a loaded package contained in the search path, you must enter the corresponding package name with the prefix “package:” (a colon) as an argument. For example, the following function call lists all (exported) functions available in the stringr package after loading the package with library(stringr):

> ls("package:stringr")

The RGui IDE is rarely used, but there are some useful cases. An example is the function call help.start() , which invokes the HTML help with the preferred browser (in my case, Mozilla’s Firefox), which is sometimes more flexible compared to the internal RStudio help.

  1. The central elements belonging to a function can be extracted with formals, body and environment.↩︎

  2. There are no vignettes for most packages. In addition, some packages contain several vignettes, but not a single vignette name matches the library name. This is the case with ggplot2, for example, where the three very informative vignettes are named ggplot2-specs, extending-ggplot2 and ggplot2-in-packages.↩︎

  3. In the context of this course, two functions with the same name tally are used, one from the Tidyverse package dplyr, the other from the package mosaic. To avoid naming conflicts, we will only ever load the Tidyverse libraries and use the prefix form mosaic::tally when using the tally function from mosaic.↩︎
